01-001.r: India → about 2.4% of world area; 7th largest (3.28 million sq km), not 6th; Tropic of Cancer divides it into two halves, so it is not wholly tropical.

01-002.r: India → 7th largest by area (after Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil, Australia); about 2.4% of world land area; IST meridian 82°30'E; not wholly in the torrid zone.
01-002.h: Six bigger countries: 'RCU-CBA' = Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil, Australia; India is 7th.

01-005.r: India → about 2.4% of world area but about 17% of world population (16.7% in Census 2001; 17.5% in Census 2011).

01-006.r: Villages in India (Census 2011) → 6,40,932; so 5 lakh, 6 lakh 30 thousand and 8 lakh are all wrong (None of these).

01-007.r: Wrong pair: 'states in India – 26'; India has 28 states and 8 UTs. Correct: area 3.28 million sq km; 8°4'N–37°6'N; 68°7'E–97°25'E.

01-008.r: Mainland India's latitudinal extent → 8°4'N to 37°6'N; it lies wholly in the Northern Hemisphere.

01-009.r: Wrong: earliest sunrise in Mizoram; India's first sunrise is in Arunachal Pradesh. True: 7th largest by area; land boundary about 15,200 km; most populous (UNFPA 2023).

02-001.r: India extends 8°4'N–37°6'N and 68°7'E–97°25'E; Tropic of Cancer passes almost through its middle. Options with 37°17'53'' N are wrong → None of the above.

02-002.r: The latitude passing through Sikkim also passes through Rajasthan.

02-003.r: Longitude seventy degrees East → passes through Jaisalmer (Rajasthan).

03-001.r: Tropic of Cancer → 8 states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram. 'Bihar' accepted only because Jharkhand was then part of Bihar.

03-002.r: Tropic of Cancer → 8 states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram; before 2000 that stretch was in Bihar (now Jharkhand); not Odisha, UP, Meghalaya.
03-002.h: West to east: 'GRaM ChhaJ WaT Mizo' = Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, WB, Tripura, Mizoram.

03-008.r: Town nearest the Tropic of Cancer (23°30'N) → Gandhinagar (23°19'N, only 11' away); Agartala (23°50'N) is 20' away; Jabalpur and Ujjain farther.

03-009.r: City nearest the Tropic of Cancer (23°30'N) among Delhi, Kolkata, Jodhpur, Nagpur → Kolkata (about 22°30'–22°37'N).

03-010.r: 23°30' North latitude (Tropic of Cancer) divides India into almost two equal parts.
03-010.t: Don't pick 23°30' South; the line dividing India is 23°30' North.

03-011.r: True: Tropic of Cancer splits India into two halves; line joining easternmost and westernmost points lies north of it. False: it halves the border; widest E-W extent lies along it.

03-012.r: Manipur lies wholly north of the Tropic of Cancer; the Tropic crosses Jharkhand, Mizoram and Tripura.

03-013.r: Around 21 June (summer solstice) days grow longer as you go north → Delhi (most northerly option) has a longer day than Bhopal, Hyderabad, Chennai.

03-014.r: City nearest the Tropic of Cancer among Jabalpur, Ahmedabad, Ujjain, Varanasi → Jabalpur (smallest latitude gap); Varanasi lies well north of it.

03-015.r: Mahi river → crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice; rises in MP, flows through Rajasthan and Gujarat into the Gulf of Khambhat (Arabian Sea).

04-001.r: True: mainland India spans about thirty degrees of latitude and longitude; Standard Meridian (eighty-two and a half degrees East) time is IST. False: 2½-hour Gujarat–Arunachal lag (it is 2).

04-002.r: Midnight at IST meridian (82°30'E), 6 a.m. at a place → it is 90° east (15° = 1 hour) → 172°30'E.
04-002.h: Sun rises in the east: a place ahead in time lies to the east.

04-003.r: Westernmost Gujarat village to Walong (easternmost Arunachal) → about 29°26' of longitude × 4 minutes ≈ 2 hours time difference.

04-004.r: Correct: Aurangabad's latitude lies between Vadodara and Pune; Bengaluru lies south of Chennai. Wrong: Jabalpur's longitude lies east of both Indore and Bhopal, not between them.

04-005.r: IST meridian (82°30'E; IST = GMT + 5:30) passes Mirzapur district (UP); nearest city among options → Rewa (81°02'–82°20'E); Ujjain is farthest.

04-006.r: 10:00 a.m. IST → Shillong (92°E): 92 − 82.5 = 9.5° × 4 minutes = 38 minutes ahead → local time 10:38 a.m.
04-006.h: Each 1° of longitude = 4 minutes; places east of 82.5°E are ahead of IST.

04-007.r: Noon at IST meridian (82°30'E) → at 120°E: 37°30' × 4 = 150 minutes (2 h 30 min) ahead → 14:30.

04-008.r: IST meridian → passes through UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh; not Maharashtra.
04-008.h: North to south 'U-M-C-O-A': UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Andhra.

04-009.r: Standard Meridian 82°30'E → passes Mirzapur district (near Prayagraj), UP; IST = GMT + 5 hours 30 minutes.
04-009.t: Don't pick Allahabad/Prayagraj: the meridian passes Mirzapur district nearby. The book gives no single answer (*).

04-013.r: Tirap (Arunachal, 95°31'E) and Kandla (Gujarat, 70°11'E) → about 2 hours apart; sunrise 5:00 a.m. at Tirap → about 7:00 a.m. at Kandla.

04-014.r: City on a longitude closest to Delhi's → Bengaluru (77°19'–77°50'E); Hyderabad, Nagpur and Pune lie farther east or west.

04-015.r: Tropic of Cancer and IST meridian intersect in Koria district, Chhattisgarh → Baghelkhand plateau.

05-001.r: Southernmost point of India → Indira Point, Great Nicobar (Nicobar district, A&N Islands); mainland's southernmost point → Kanyakumari, Tamil Nadu (8°4'N).
05-001.t: Don't confuse Indira Point (south, Great Nicobar) with the northernmost point near Siachen Glacier.

05-004.r: Easternmost state → Arunachal Pradesh; westernmost state → Gujarat.

05-005.r: Westernmost point of India → west of Guhar Moti in Kutch, Gujarat; longitude 68°7' East (not West).

05-006.r: Most eastward among Hyderabad, Bhopal, Lucknow, Bengaluru → Lucknow (80°34'–81°12'E); Bhopal is the most westward.

05-007.r: Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu), southernmost point of the mainland → where the Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean meet.

06-001.r: All correct: Assam borders Bhutan and Bangladesh; West Bengal borders Bhutan, Nepal (and Bangladesh); Mizoram borders Bangladesh and Myanmar.

06-003.r: States bordering Bangladesh → West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram; not Manipur (borders Myanmar) or Nagaland.
06-003.h: 'MATM + WB': Meghalaya, Assam, Tripura, Mizoram and West Bengal.

06-006.r: States bordering Bhutan → West Bengal, Sikkim, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh; not Meghalaya (borders Bangladesh) or Bihar.
06-006.h: Bhutan's neighbours 'SAWA': Sikkim, Arunachal, West Bengal, Assam.

06-008.r: Composite Dialogue (November 1998) map → A Sir Creek: boundary dispute; B LOC region: troop disengagement; C: river-water sharing (Wullar Barrage/Tulbul project).

06-009.r: Longest border with Myanmar → Arunachal Pradesh; Myanmar-border states → Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram.
06-009.h: North to south 'ANMM': Arunachal, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram.

06-011.r: Assam has no border with Myanmar (it borders Bangladesh and Bhutan); Myanmar touches Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram.

06-012.r: States/UTs bordering Pakistan → Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab, Rajasthan, Gujarat; not Himachal Pradesh or Haryana.

06-013.r: States bordering Nepal → Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Sikkim; so the pair is Sikkim–Bihar.
06-013.h: West to east 'U-U-B-W-S': Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, WB, Sikkim.

06-014.r: Longest land frontier with India → Bangladesh (4096.7 km); bordered by Mizoram, Tripura, Assam, Meghalaya, West Bengal.

06-015.r: India–Pakistan boundary → Radcliffe Line (also India–Bangladesh); Durand Line → Afghanistan; McMahon Line → China; Maginot Line → France–Germany.

06-016.r: Radcliffe Line → India–Pakistan (and India–Bangladesh) boundary; Durand Line → boundary with Afghanistan.
06-016.t: Don't confuse Radcliffe (Pakistan) with Durand (Afghanistan) or McMahon (China).

06-018.r: India–Pakistan boundary (Radcliffe Line, 1947) → superimposed boundary: one imposed on an area by an outsider or conquering power.

06-019.r: McMahon Line → India–China boundary; result of the Shimla Treaty of 1914; named after Sir Henry McMahon.

06-020.r: India–China boundary line → McMahon Line, drawn by Sir Henry McMahon.
06-020.t: Radcliffe Line → Pakistan; Durand Line → Afghanistan; Indira Point is a place, not a line.

06-021.r: McMahon Line (Simla Convention, 3 July 1914) → boundary between Arunachal Pradesh and south-eastern China.

06-024.r: India and Sri Lanka are separated by the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar.

06-025.r: Sikkim → borders three countries: Nepal, Bhutan and China.

06-026.r: Tripura → international border (Bangladesh) on three sides: north, west, south; Assam and Mizoram lie to its east.

06-027.r: Land border: Bangladesh 4096.7 km > China 3488 > Pakistan 3323 > Nepal 1751 > Myanmar 1643 > Bhutan 699 > Afghanistan 106 (total 15,106.7).
06-027.h: Ascending order asked: Nepal < Pakistan < China < Bangladesh.

06-028.r: India's territorial sea → 12 nautical miles (about 22.2 km) from the coast.

06-029.r: Uttarakhand districts on the Tibet border → Uttarkashi, Chamoli, Pithoragarh; Almora is not.

07-001.r: Paleomagnetic results (record of Earth's magnetic field in rocks) → the Indian landmass has moved northward.

07-002.r: Indian subcontinent was part of Gondwana, which broke up about 200 million years ago → Africa, South America, Australia, Antarctica, Peninsular India, Arabia.

07-003.r: India → 4 natural regions: Northern Mountains, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Coasts and Islands; split further into 6 (adds Indian Desert; coasts and islands separate).

07-004.r: Deccan Traps: lower trap about 150 m, middle about 1200 m, upper about 450 m deep. Wrong pair: intertrappean beds – fossils of sea plants and animals.

07-005.r: Artesian well (water rises without a pump, by aquifer pressure) → in Uttarakhand found mostly in the Tarai region.

07-006.r: True: Meghalaya plateau extends the Peninsular plateau; Kashmir valley formed in a synclinorium; Ganga plain in a foredeep. False: Himalayas from Indian–European–Chinese plate triple convergence.

07-007.r: Wrong: west coast formed by river deposits (it formed by submergence and emergence of land). True: Peninsula is oldest; Himalaya youngest fold mountains; Gondwana rocks hold most coal.

07-008.r: Deccan Traps → Cretaceous-Eocene; Western Ghats → Late Cenozoic; Aravalli → Pre-Cambrian; Narmada-Tapti alluvium → Pleistocene.

07-009.r: Kuttanad (Kerala) → lowest-altitude region of India, farmed 1.2–3.0 m below sea level; 'Rice Bowl of Kerala'; FAO Agricultural Heritage System.

07-010.r: Desert region among the options → Sindhu (Indus Valley) area, in north-western Punjab Province (Pakistan).

07-011.r: Dharwar rocks in Bihar → Munger, Nawada, Jamui (south-east Bihar); Rohtas (south-west, Kaimur–Son valley) has Vindhyan formations, not Dharwar.

07-012.r: Youngest rock system among Dharwar, Cuddapah, Vindhyan, Gondwana → Gondwana; Dharwar formed from Archean rocks, Cuddapah after Dharwar.
07-012.h: Old to young 'D-C-V-G': Dharwar, Cuddapah, Vindhyan, Gondwana.

07-013.r: Statement I false: J.D. Dana's Manual of Geology covers America (he coined 'Archaean'). II true: T.S. Holland split Indian rocks into Archaean, Purana, Dravidian, Aryan.

07-014.r: Ganga Plain → described as a geosyncline (trough where sediment piles up); peneplain = level erosion surface; pediplain = joined pediments.

07-015.r: Indian (Thar) desert → lies west of the Aravallis; rainfall below 150 mm a year; Luni is its only large river. All statements correct.

08-001.r: A true: Himalayan rivers are perennial (glacier-fed). R true: Himalaya gets most rain from the south-west monsoon. But R does not explain A.

08-002.r: Only statement 1 is correct: the Himalayan region has huge hydroelectric potential (perennial rivers, steep gradients, narrow valleys). Statement 2 about eastern UP and Bihar is wrong.

08-003.r: Himalayas are still rising (about 5 mm a year) because the Indian plate is colliding with the Eurasian plate → A and R true; R explains A.

08-005.r: Himalayas are the source of large perennial rivers because their higher ranges stay snow-covered all year → A and R true; R explains A.

08-006.r: Oldest Himalayan range → Great Himalaya (Oligocene, 37–24 million years ago); then Middle Himalaya (Miocene); Shiwalik (Pliocene) youngest.
08-006.h: Age falls going south: Great → Middle → Shiwalik.

08-007.r: Without the Himalayas → Siberian cold waves over India; Indo-Gangetic plain without vast alluvium; a different monsoon pattern. All three correct.

08-008.r: Bhabar → flat pebbly belt (8–16 km wide) along the Shiwalik foothills; so porous that streams vanish underground.
08-008.t: Don't confuse Bhabar (pebble belt at foothills) with Tarai, Doon or Khadar.

08-009.r: Shiwalik range → mainly unconsolidated sediments: river-borne pebbles, gravel, alluvium, sand and clay.

08-010.r: Foothills of the Himalayas → Shiwalik, the outermost range; 10–50 km wide, 900–1100 m high.

08-012.r: Shiwalik (outer Himalaya, outermost range) → formed about 2–5 million years ago in the Pliocene epoch, Cenozoic era.

08-015.r: Shiwalik range (about 2500 km long) → average height 900–1100 m, varying by region. The book gives no single answer (*).

08-016.r: Kumaon Himalaya → between Satluj and Kali; Punjab Himalaya: Indus–Satluj; Nepal Himalaya: Kali–Teesta; Assam Himalaya: Teesta–Dihang.
08-016.h: West to east 'P-K-N-A': Punjab, Kumaon, Nepal, Assam.

08-017.r: Bhabar (8–16 km belt of boulders south of Shiwalik) → example of a piedmont situation; Tarai (15–30 km wide) lies south of it.

08-018.r: North-Western Himalaya → Zanskar; Himachal–Uttarakhand Himalaya → Shivalik Range; Darjeeling–Sikkim Himalaya → Lepcha tribe; Arunachal Himalaya → Namcha Barwa.

08-019.r: Evidence that the Himalayas are young fold mountains → deep gorges, U-turn river courses, parallel ranges, steep slopes with landslides (all four).

08-020.r: Jammu and Kashmir map, ranges 1 to 4 → Karakoram, Ladakh, Zanskar, Pir Panjal (north to south).

08-021.r: Ranges north to south → Karakoram, Ladakh, Zanskar, Shiwalik.
08-021.h: K-L-Z run in alphabet order from north to south; Shiwalik at the foothills.

08-022.r: Lesser (Middle) Himalaya, also called Himachal → between the Shiwalik (south) and Great Himalaya (north); average width about 50 km.

08-023.r: Western Himalaya, south to north → Shiwalik → Lesser Himalaya → Great Himalaya.

08-024.r: Youngest mountain chain → Shiwaliks (outer Himalaya, formed last); Vindhyas, Aravalli and Annamalai are much older.

08-025.r: South to north → Dhauladhar (Lesser Himalaya), Zanskar, Ladakh, Karakoram (last three are Trans-Himalaya).
08-025.h: Going north after Dhauladhar: Z, L, K (alphabet in reverse).

08-026.r: Northward sequence → Pir Panjal (Middle Himalaya), Zanskar, Ladakh, Karakoram (Trans-Himalaya).

08-027.r: Peaks east to west → Kanchenjunga, Everest, Annapurna, Dhaulagiri; Kanchenjunga (world's third tallest) lies on the Sikkim–Nepal border.

08-028.r: Youngest range among the options → Patkai range (Tertiary era); Ajanta, Palkonda and Kaimur are old ranges of South and Central India.

08-029.r: Patkai hills (India–Myanmar border) → Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland; not Tripura (it has the Mizo hills).

08-030.r: Pir Panjal Range → Middle Himalaya, in Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir (south-east to north-west).
